Macrons

Consonantal i

Tools, fasteners & household repair

hook onto verb

also fasten with a hook

our formation

uncō affīgere

fasten with a hook

Our descriptive phrase. uncō can also be the dative “to a hook”; the construction and context determine the relation. The two English verb senses (hook onto, catch with a hook) are expressed compositionally; neither phrase is presented as a separately verified technical headword.

Examples

  • Hoc huic uncō affīge.

    Hook this onto this hook / attach this to this hook.composed

  • Theodōrus bacillum aduncum ex trānsversāriō māchinae suspendit.

    Theo hung the hooked stick from the scaffold’s crossbar.composed

Other words

  • affīgō, affīgere, affīxī, affīxum — fasten or attach

    verb, third conjugation · also used · classical

    affīgere emphasizes attachment or fastening; it is not a universal equivalent of English “hook.” Choose the verb according to the action and result.

  • suspendō, suspendere — hang up, suspend

    verb, third conjugation · also used · classical · Verg. G. 2.389: oscilla ex altā suspendunt mollia pīnū

    For hooking something over a bar and leaving it hanging, as in the composed example of the stick on the scaffolding; compare Vergil for suspendere ex + ablative. trānsversārium is Vitruvius’s crosspiece; a scaffold tube is not a vectis (lever, crowbar).

See also hook, catch with a hook, upright.

SourcesLewis & Short: affigo · Lewis & Short: suspendo · Lewis & Short: transversarius

The example sentences marked “composed” are ours.
